name: Iconoir
tagline: 1,671 MIT-licensed SVG icons on a 24px grid, with React, Vue and Flutter packages
description: Iconoir is an open-source icon library of 1,671 icons drawn on a 24x24 pixel grid, published under the MIT licence with no attribution requirement. It ships as plain SVG plus first-party packages for React, React Native, Vue, Flutter and Swift, a CSS icon font, and Figma and Framer libraries. It is the pick when you want a broad, genuinely free icon set that is not Lucide or Heroicons, and its stroke weight sits slightly heavier and rounder than Lucide's.
agent_guidance: Reach for Iconoir when the project needs an icon that Lucide or Heroicons does not have, or when you want a second set whose 24px grid and stroke weight will not clash with a Lucide-based system. Install `iconoir-react` and import named components; the CSS-font route via jsDelivr is only worth it for non-bundled static HTML. MIT with no attribution clause means you can recolour, restyle and ship it commercially without any licence bookkeeping.
why_it_matters: One of the few large icon sets that is truly MIT and multi-framework, so it drops into a codebase without a licence conversation.
notable_for: React, React Native, Vue, Flutter, Swift packages

name: css.gg
tagline: 704 icons drawn in pure CSS — but the licence since v2.1.2 forbids commercial use
description: css.gg is an icon library of roughly 700 UI icons built almost entirely from CSS pseudo-elements and box-shadows rather than SVG paths, so each icon inherits colour and size from the surrounding CSS. The repository also ships SVG and Figma versions, and the author's companion project GLYF*APP claims 6,000+ glyphs. The critical caveat is licensing: versions before 2.1.2 were MIT, but the current licence restricts use to personal, non-commercial projects, requires attribution to the author and the brand, and forbids derivative works.
pricing_detail: Free to download; commercial use requires written permission from the author.
agent_guidance: Do not add css.gg to a commercial product without checking with the user first — the LICENSE.md in the repo restricts use to personal, non-commercial projects, requires brand attribution, and bans derivative works. If the user wants CSS-only icons that avoid an SVG payload, this is the reference implementation of the technique, but pinning `css.gg@2.1.1` or earlier is the only way to stay on the old MIT terms. For anything shipping to customers, prefer Iconoir or Lucide instead.
why_it_matters: The best-known demonstration that a whole icon set can be drawn in CSS, and a cautionary example of an MIT library relicensed to non-commercial mid-life.
notable_for: relicensed from MIT to non-commercial at v2.1.2
SVG and Figma versions alongside the CSS
evidence: https://css.gg, https://api.github.com/repos/astrit/css.gg, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astrit/css.gg/master/LICENSE.md, https://registry.npmjs.org/css.gg, GitHub contents API count of icons/svg

name: Streamline
tagline: 447,000+ icons in 34 families, plus illustrations, with an API and an MCP server
description: Streamline is a commercial icon and illustration catalogue of about 447,000 assets organised into 34 families and 172 sets, spanning its own styles (Ultimate, Core, Flex, Sharp, Plump, Micro, Freehand, Nova, Cyber, Vault) and mirrored open-source sets such as Lucide, Phosphor, Tabler, Feather, Carbon and Material Symbols. Beyond the web app it ships a Figma plugin, VS Code, Webflow, Framer, Miro and Lucid plugins, a REST API and an MCP server. Access is subscription or one-time lifetime purchase per set, with roughly 9,000 free assets at /freebies.
pricing_detail: Full Access from $29/mo (360,000+ assets); Icons from $19/mo (300,000+ icons, 55 sets); Illustrations from $19/mo (30,000 across 11 sets); Elements from $9/mo (12,500 across 37 sets). Yearly billing saves up to 40%. One-time lifetime purchase available per set. Free tier at streamlinehq.com/freebies. API and MCP capped at 1,000 assets/week.
agent_guidance: This is the one paid icon catalogue with an MCP server, so if the user already has a Streamline subscription, wire the MCP up and search assets in-conversation instead of scraping the site. Without a subscription, treat it as reference only and fall back to Lucide or Iconoir — the free freebies tier is small and the per-project caps (100 icons, 50 illustrations) bite on anything real. Also note that plain curl hits a Vercel Security Checkpoint on streamlinehq.com, so headless scraping of the catalogue will fail.
why_it_matters: The largest coherent commercial icon system, and the only one that has shipped an MCP server so an agent can search it directly.
notable_for: Figma, VS Code, Webflow, Framer plugins
Vercel Security Checkpoint blocks plain curl
evidence: https://www.streamlinehq.com/ (via WebFetch; plain curl returned 429 behind a Vercel Security Checkpoint), https://home.streamlinehq.com/pricing, web search for family and set counts

name: Icons8
tagline: ~1.3M icons in 47 styles, free only under CC BY-ND with a mandatory backlink
description: Icons8 is a very large asset marketplace covering icons (roughly 1.3 million, drawn in 47 matched UI styles), plus stock photos, vector illustrations, music and AI tools such as an upscaler and background remover. Free downloads are permitted commercially but only under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs 3.0 licence that requires a visible link back to icons8.com and forbids modifying the artwork; paid plans remove both constraints. There is a documented REST API at developers.icons8.com, and the company also makes the Lunacy design tool.
pricing_detail: Per-asset-type subscriptions from about $24/mo each (icons, photos, illustrations, music); all-in bundle around $89/mo; roughly 20% off annually. Free tier requires a CC BY-ND backlink to icons8.com. API is separately metered by monthly downloads and calls.
agent_guidance: Two hard blockers: icons8.com sits behind a Cloudflare interstitial that returns 403 to every automated fetch, and the free licence is Attribution-NoDerivs, so you may not recolour or edit an icon and you must render a visible credit link. Do not silently drop Icons8 assets into a product build; if the user has a paid plan, use the developers.icons8.com API instead of the site, and note its terms forbid caching responses. For anything an agent needs to fetch, restyle, or ship without attribution, Iconoir, Lucide or Phosphor are the correct choices.
why_it_matters: The biggest icon catalogue on the web, and the clearest case where scale does not translate into usability for an automated workflow.
notable_for: free tier is CC BY-ND with mandatory backlink
metered REST API that forbids caching
also ships the Lunacy design app
evidence: https://icons8.com (403 Cloudflare challenge on two attempts via WebFetch and curl), https://icons8.com/license (403), https://developers.icons8.com/pricing (fetched OK), web search for icon count and licence terms

name: Google Fonts
tagline: 1,942 open-licensed families with a free CDN and a public metadata endpoint
description: Google Fonts is the default open-source webfont catalogue: 1,942 families as of August 2026, broken down as 717 sans-serif, 467 display, 358 handwriting, 349 serif and 51 monospace. Almost every family is under the SIL Open Font Licence, with about 44 under Apache 2.0 and 5 under the Ubuntu Font Licence, so the fonts are free to self-host, subset, modify and ship commercially. Delivery is via the fonts.googleapis.com/css2 endpoint or direct download, and the whole catalogue is queryable as JSON.

github.license: OFL-1.1 (per family; also Apache-2.0 and UFL)

agent_guidance: The browse UI at fonts.google.com is a JavaScript shell and returns nothing useful to a fetcher — hit https://fonts.google.com/metadata/fonts instead, which is an unauthenticated JSON list of every family with its category, axes, subsets, designers and popularity rank (strip the anti-JSON-hijack prefix before the first brace). Use the css2 endpoint for quick prototypes, but for production prefer self-hosting or Fontsource, since the Google CDN adds a third-party request and gives no caching benefit across sites. The OFL terms let you subset and modify freely, so variable-axis subsetting is fair game.
why_it_matters: The licence floor for web typography — if a font is here, you can ship it anywhere without a EULA conversation.
notable_for: OFL for almost the entire catalogue
evidence: https://fonts.google.com/ (JS shell, no readable content), https://fonts.google.com/metadata/fonts (parsed: 1,942 families with category breakdown), https://developers.google.com/fonts/docs/developer_api, https://api.github.com/repos/google/fonts/contents/{ofl,apache,ufl}, https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2 (200)

name: Fonts In Use
tagline: 34,302 documented typography specimens, indexed by typeface, format and industry
description: Fonts In Use is an independent archive of typography in the wild: 34,302 catalogued examples of real design work, each annotated with the typefaces identified in it. It is cross-indexed three ways — 37 industry topics (Music 6,723, Art 5,024, Event 3,428, Food/Beverage 3,254 and so on), 21 formats (Branding/Identity 9,066, Books 6,971, Posters/Flyers 6,122, Web 5,982), and by typeface (Futura 1,232 uses, Helvetica 1,508, Univers 651). It has run since December 2010 and accepts public submissions, with 6,331 entries marked as staff picks.
agent_guidance: Unlike Dribbble or Behance, this one is genuinely readable — the pages are server-rendered HTML with the typeface names, designers and commentary in the markup, so a plain fetch of a topic or typeface URL returns real text you can reason over. Use it to answer 'what type do record sleeves / municipal signage / literary presses actually use', then map the answer to a licensable equivalent, because most of the typefaces catalogued here are commercial foundry releases, not Google Fonts. The images are third-party works with no reuse licence, so cite and link rather than copy.
why_it_matters: The only serious evidence base for typographic decisions — it replaces taste-arguments with a searchable record of what practitioners actually set.
notable_for: indexed by 37 topics, 21 formats and 150+ typefaces
evidence: https://fontsinuse.com (curl 200, 214KB HTML, taxonomy and counts parsed directly from markup), https://fontsinuse.com/about
